extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York / citizens considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution (1788)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and normative arguments about the proper structure, membership, apportionment, and terms of the federal House of Representatives under the proposed U.S. Constitution, aimed at informing citizens' judgment on ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualifications of the electors are 'to be the same with those of the electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition of the right of suffrage is 'very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government.' The Convention should fix this in the Constitution rather than leave it to Congress or State legislative discretion; using the State standard is 'the best that lay within their option' because it is familiar to the States and not alterable by State governments in a way that would undermine federal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of representatives (age, citizenship, residence, office)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative must 'be of the age of twenty-five years; must have been seven years a citizen of the United States; must, at the time of his election, be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent; and, during the time of his service, must be in no office under the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'reasonable limitations' intended to keep the door open to merit 'whether native or adoptive' and without regard to wealth, profession, or religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing suffrage in the Constitution rather than leaving it to Congress or States
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of suffrage should be defined and established in the Constitution rather than left to occasional regulation by Congress or to the legislative discretion of the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving suffrage undefined would render the federal branch too dependent on State governments or Congress; fixing it in the Constitution secures it as a fundamental article of republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections — dependence and sympathy with the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections are 'the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectually secured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How frequent is necessary cannot be precisely calculated and depends on circumstances; experience suggests that biennial elections under the federal system 'cannot possibly be dangerous to the requisite dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents' given the federal context and collateral legislative checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial elections — balance of safety and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Biennial elections will be 'as useful to the affairs of the public as ... safe to the liberty of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in favor: representatives need time in office to acquire practical knowledge of diverse federal matters (state laws, commerce, militia, foreign affairs); two years better proportioned to required knowledge than one. Practical considerations (travel burdens, stability of service) and reduced encouragement of illicit returns also favor a longer term than annual elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent as guidance (Commons, Ireland, colonies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use historical examples (House of Commons, Ireland, colonial assemblies) to judge appropriate election frequency and legislative durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English experience moved from annual sessions to triennial and finally septennial returns; colonial American experience varied from one to seven years with no evidence that biennial elections would imperil liberty. Historical precedent should inform but not dictate exact choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of legislative power to term length
rubrics_metrics.description: Where legislative power is greater, its duration ought to be shorter; conversely, smaller powers may safely have longer duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal legislature will possess only part of supreme legislative authority (unlike the British Parliament), and will be checked by state legislatures, which supports the safety of biennial terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for representatives' practical knowledge (including foreign affairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal representatives ought to possess knowledge of the laws and public affairs of all States and some knowledge of foreign affairs and the law of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of this knowledge 'can only be derived from the public sources of information' and 'will be acquired to best effect by a practical attention to the subject during the period of actual service in the legislature,' supporting longer terms than at the State level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical considerations favoring longer terms (travel, re-election norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance and travel burdens, and differences in re-election conventions between State assemblies and popular elections, make longer terms (two years) more practicable and less discouraging to suitable candidates than one-year terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates to existing Congress were re-elected as a matter of course by legislatures; popular elections might not follow that pattern, so a longer term reduces the hardship and disincentive for capable persons to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of illicit returns with very frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Very frequent elections (e.g., annual) increase the opportunity for 'unlawful means' to obtain irregular returns because there may be insufficient time to investigate and annul spurious elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each house judges elections and qualifications; if annual terms prevent timely correction of illegitimate members, illicit incentives grow—biennial terms reduce that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of representatives by population (same rule as direct taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appointment of members among the States is 'to be determined by the same rule with that of direct taxes'—i.e., by the number of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers are the natural standard for representation (personal rights) even if they are an imperfect measure for taxation (property); using the same rule for both representation and taxation creates countervailing incentives that promote accuracy in the census.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of slaves in the census (mixed character rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves are viewed in the Constitution as having a 'mixed character of persons and of property' and therefore the Constitution 'regards them as inhabitants, but as debased by servitude below the equal level of free inhabitants,' leading to the compromising expedient (three-fifths-type reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: slaves partake in some legal respects of personhood and in others of property; Southern States could claim inconsistency if slaves counted for taxation but not representation. The compromise treats slaves as inhabitants but 'divested of two fifths of the man,' balancing opposing incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of property/wealth in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation should pay 'some attention ... to property in the choice' of hands entrusted with government because government protects property as well as persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the federal level property-rights interests are committed to the same representatives as personal rights; since states cannot influence each other's representation, any advantage from greater wealth should be secured by superior share of representation. Thus, proportional representation by numbers plus regard to wealth is defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a common rule for representation and taxation to balance state incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the same rule (aggregate number of inhabitants) to both representation and taxation will produce opposite incentives for States to exaggerate or understate population, 'which will control and balance each other, and produce the requisite impartiality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because census accuracy depends on state co-operation, tying both representation and taxation to the same measure reduces bias and manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria and concerns for the total number of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding the total number of Representatives must weigh whether the House will be 'an unsafe depositary of the public interests' if too small, whether members will lack knowledge of local circumstances, whether they will be drawn from a class at odds with the mass, and whether initial numbers will become disproportionate as population grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No precise solution exists; comparisons among States show large variance in representative-to-constituent ratios. The question requires balancing local familiarity, class representation, practical governance, and growth dynamics rather than a one-size-fits-all formula.
